title: Chapter 69
content:
A sharp, persistent knock shattered the silence of the master suite.

Il-hyun’s eyes opened in the dark. He sat up, checking the glowing digital numerals of the nightstand clock: exactly 06:00. Sliding out from beneath the sheets, he crossed the hardwood floor and opened the door.

Park Tae-soo was standing on the threshold.

The look etched into his security chief’s face was one Il-hyun hadn't seen since the morning he took two sniper rounds through his thighs at the inauguration a year ago. For an immovable, stone-faced veteran like Tae-soo to look this rattled, something had gone catastrophically wrong.

Without asking, Il-hyun grabbed a black silk robe from the armchair, throwing it over his bare torso.

Following Tae-soo down the grand staircase, the senior housekeeper emerged from the kitchen with an anxious, fretful expression. Leaving her behind, Il-hyun strode through the double doors and out past the front gates.

A cluster of night-shift sentries stood gathered around a parked vehicle on the driveway.

It was the reinforced sedan Jakyeong had taken for yesterday’s contract—an armored fortress equipped with ballistic glass and plated chassis. Standing stiffly beside it with their hands clasped behind their backs were Park Sung-soo and the two operatives assigned to yesterday's surveillance detail.

The three men bowed at the waist, their posture radiating the grim resolve of soldiers preparing for ritual execution.

"Our deepest apologies, President Kang. This failure rests entirely on our incompetence. We relied solely on the vehicle's GPS beacon without physically verifying the driver. We will accept whatever punishment you deem fit."

Il-hyun’s gaze drifted past them.

Kneeling on the cold asphalt, trembling and sobbing hysterically, was a man he had never seen before. A guard hauled the stranger up by his collar, only for the man’s knees to buckle in terror.

"I swear to God, I don't know anything!" the driver wailed, pressing his palms together in frantic supplication. "Some guys just tossed me a stack of cash and told me to park the car right here! That's all I did! Please, have mercy! Spare my life!"

Scattered across the pavement before him was a loose, rubber-banded brick of foreign currency.

Il-hyun walked slowly toward the rear of the sedan. The reinforced glass bore multiple white, spiderwebbed bullet fractures—clear proof of the firefight from the night before.

"Open it," Il-hyun said, his voice dropping into an arctic register.

A subordinate scrambled to pop the trunk.

Resting inside the compartment were the tactical vests, combat boots, suppressed firearms, and discarded civilian clothes the three operatives had been issued.

Il-hyun reached into the pocket of his robe, drawing out his personal phone.

He selected the contact saved under the name Darling and hit dial.

A muffled vibration buzzed from deep within the trunk: Bzzzt. Bzzzt.

Tae-soo reached in, retrieving the brand-new flagship device Il-hyun had gifted Jakyeong only yesterday afternoon. Tae-soo's eyes caught the glowing screen, his hand freezing for a fraction of a second before extending the handset across.

Il-hyun took the device.

Illuminating the display of Jakyeong's phone, the incoming caller ID read a single, unambiguous title:

The Bastard

A dry, incredulous chuckle slipped past Il-hyun's lips.

The irony was so sharp it was almost comedic. Holding the two screens side-by-side laid the reality bare: on one side, Darling; on the other, The Bastard. It was a brutal, unvarnished summary of their dynamic—and a glaring testament to how thoroughly he had indulged in his own pathetic delusions.

He had assumed the boy's refusal to sign the contract was merely playing hard to get. He had personally walked into a boutique florist for the first time in his life, spent an eternity selecting the perfect arrangement of dark roses, and brought them home convinced he was making progress.

He had even scouted and privately reserved an exclusive restaurant for two just to share lunch today.

A fool. A monumental, certified idiot.

Il-hyun closed his eyes against the rising heat in his chest.

Tae-soo stepped forward, his head bowed. "I have already ordered full surveillance sweeps of every intersection and toll plaza within a fifty-kilometer radius. They cannot have traveled far. I will drag them back personally, sir."

When Il-hyun opened his eyes, the warmth had vanished entirely, replaced by a venomous, unblinking malice.

He placed a cigarette between his lips and sparked the flame. He stood in absolute, suffocating silence, drawing smoke until the paper burned down to the filter, his dark eyes boring into the empty vehicle. The air around him felt cold enough to freeze blood.

Snubbing the ember against the heel of his palm, Il-hyun addressed his security chief. His voice was terrifyingly calm—a stillness far more dangerous than an outright roar.

"Lock down every international terminal and maritime port in the country. Find him before he clears the border."

Without waiting for an answer, he tossed Jakyeong’s phone into the trunk with a dismissive flick and disappeared back into the estate.

The three disgraced tail operatives let out long, shuddering breaths of relief. Tae-soo ordered the weeping civilian released, then began barking tactical commands into his radio.
After a two-hour transit aboard a battered fishing trawler, the skiff pulled up against the rocky shoreline of an isolated offshore island.

The moment the hull ground against the gravel, Jakyeong, Wang Han, and Wang Ryun worked in synchronized silence, hauling their heavy tactical duffels and supply crates onto the rocks. Once the cargo was ashore, Han handed a thick envelope of cash to the weathered old captain, who gave a silent nod and steered the vessel back into open water.

As the trawler melted into the morning haze, the three turned to inspect their surroundings.

Pulling his cap low, Jakyeong’s brow pinched into an instant scowl.

He had envisioned a secluded coastal sanctuary; instead, the shoreline was choked with endless piles of marine flotsam washed ashore by the tides. Rusted plastic basins, tangled nylon nets, cracked rubber boots, discarded glass bottles, and dented industrial oil drums littered the rocks.

Less of a private retreat and more of a floating landfill.

"Let's move the gear inside," Han said, hoisting two crates onto his broad shoulders.

Laden with cash reserves, dry provisions, and tactical hardware, the trio pushed into the dense island foliage. The untamed brush had swallowed whatever footpaths once existed, forcing them to wade through thigh-high weeds for ten minutes before reaching a weathered wooden cabin nestled beneath a cluster of pines.

The structure was compact, but solid enough to weather heavy coastal gales.

Prying the warped door open, the rusted iron hinges groaned loudly, sending a shower of fine dust cascading from the frame.

According to Ryun, the cabin had been built years ago by an underworld contact to cook synthetic narcotics far from maritime patrols. The man had long since caught a fatal round in the chest, but Ryun had remembered the coordinates from a single visit a decade prior.

Setting the bags in the corner, Han threw open the wooden shutters to let the ocean breeze flush out the stale, stagnant air. Though they didn't plan on lingering indefinitely, making the shelter habitable was a priority.

Ryun bumped Jakyeong’s shoulder with a grin. "Look at that—your dream finally came true. How does it feel? You've been dying to live on an island, haven't you?"

Jakyeong shoved his arm away. "This isn't an island. It's an abandoned rock."

There was no running water, no electrical grid, and zero means of extraction without a scheduled boat. He ran two fingers across the rough-hewn table, brushing away layers of grime. Still... with a bit of sweeping, it might be tolerable.

"Are you certain the captain won't talk?" Jakyeong asked, glancing toward the sea.

"He's known across the southern docks for keeping his mouth shut," Ryun assured him. "Besides, the old man recognized my face the second I stepped onto the pier."

Han chuckled from the window. "Your face isn't exactly easy to forget."

"Neither is yours, Han-ge. Don't forget we share the same bone structure."

"Wei," Han called out, turning with an amused smirk. "Settle this. Which of us is the better-looking brother?"

Without a beat of hesitation, Jakyeong pointed straight at Wang Han.

"Traitor!" Ryun barked, lunging to wrap a playful headlock around Jakyeong’s neck. "You always side with the oldest!"

Jakyeong kicked at his shin to break the hold, laughing.

While the two bickered, Han methodically organized their provisions. The strategy was simple: lie low on this forgotten rock until the manhunt in Seoul frayed, then slip onto an international freighter bound for Southeast Asia. Ryun’s girlfriend had already boarded a commercial flight under a clean passport, and the three had zero intention of ever setting foot in Korea again.

Jakyeong hauled the dust-caked furniture outside, beating the cushions with a pine branch. Clouds of gray powder billowed into the salt air. I'll die of lung rot before Kang Il-hyun ever tracks me down.

With all three working together, the cabin was soon swept clean and orderly. It was far from a five-star suite, but it offered something infinitely more valuable: uninterrupted peace of mind.

Stepping out onto the porch, Jakyeong looked out across the canopy of pines. The vibrant, untamed green was soothing to the eyes.

Inevitably, his thoughts drifted back to Kang Il-hyun.

The man had likely anticipated an escape attempt eventually—though he probably hadn't expected them to pull the cord within hours of their very first hit. Right now, the corporate heir was undoubtedly tearing Seoul apart with bloodshot, homicidal eyes.

A faint, fleeting pang of guilt pulled at his chest.

Yet when he weighed the scales, Il-hyun had brought this on himself. The man had abducted him back to Korea, held his brother hostage, and forced an extortionate contract down his throat.

Placing a cigarette between his lips, Jakyeong looked out toward the horizon.

The evening sky had caught fire, streaked in breathtaking bands of deep amber, violet, and gold.

"Han-ge, Ryun-ge. Come look at this."

Han and Ryun stepped onto the porch. Side by side, the three operatives leaned against the wooden railing, smoking in quiet, reverent awe as the sun melted into the dark ocean swell.

Everything was still. It was remarkably peaceful.

A shared, quiet satisfaction settled over them. They had no idea how many days they’d be stranded on this rock, but treating it as an impromptu vacation didn't seem half bad.

Retreating inside as darkness fell, they assembled dinner over a portable butane burner. Even basic instant noodles and cured meats tasted extraordinary with a splash of high-proof liquor. They traded old stories late into the night until the conversation naturally tapered off.

Jakyeong stepped outside to take in the midnight sky. Unclouded by city lights, a vast, glittering tapestry of stars stretched across the black dome above.

The screen door creaked open behind him. It was Wang Han, extending a fresh cigarette.

"Why are you still awake?"

"Just enjoying the air," Jakyeong replied, accepting the smoke. "The stars are nice."

Han looked up at the sky, exhaling a quiet hum of agreement.

From inside the cabin, Ryun’s earth-shaking snores rattled through the thin timber walls. The two exchanged a wry look, shaking their heads in unison. When Wang Ryun went under, a bomb could detonate beside his cot without disturbing his sleep.

"No chance of sleeping through that tonight," Han muttered.

"None at all."

Jakyeong smiled, but Han was studying his profile with a heavy, searching gaze—a look carrying equal parts brotherly warmth and deep, protective worry.

"Wei."

"Yeah?"

"Are you holding up alright?"

"About what?"

"Just... wondering if you had any regrets."

Jakyeong understood the unspoken question immediately, his brow furrowing in sharp defensiveness.

"Why would I ever regret walking away from that psychotic bastard?"

"If you say so," Han murmured gently, patting his shoulder before turning back toward the cabin. "Get some rest soon."

Left alone beneath the starlight, Jakyeong stood scowling at the dark treeline.

What a ridiculous question. He was finally free of that lunatic. He should be feeling lighter than air.

Wang Han doesn't understand a single goddamn thing.
